method: Single printed items split from the automatic families of 1774, and of 1773 where they reach the 1774 pages (long-running ones included), every item in 3 or more papers compared by machine with every page and counted again by its opening, a sweep of word-for-word passages shared by 4 or more papers for short items the families miss, phrase searches on all 1,205 pages of 1774 in both transcriptions, reading of every hit, and scan checks of each admitted passage, by the thin-year rule (Y-THIN, as amended on 23 November 2026: an item printed by more than half of the papers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4, is eligible; the items printed by every paper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news)

new_groups.label: The act of Parliament 'for making more effectual provision for the government of the province of Quebec in North America' (the Quebec Act), as the papers printed it in September 1774

Rind's Virginia Gazette prints it headed 'A Bill intitled an Act'. Counted where the act is printed whole; abstracts of it and petitions that recite its title are not counted (C-07). The act of Parliament.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Cambridge, 29 August 1774: a letter 'said to be wrote by General Brattle' to Governor Gage, on the militia and the province's powder
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter of 29 August 1774 that the papers print as 'a Copy of a Letter, said to be wrote by General Brattle, to the Commander in chief': 'Mr. Brattle presents his Duty to his Excellency Governor Gage, he apprehends it is his Duty to acquaint his Excellency from Time to Time with every Thing he hears and knows to be true & is of Importance in these troublesome Times'; it reports that a militia captain has been pressed to warn his company to meet at a minute's warning, and that the selectmen of Medford have taken their town's stock of powder from the arsenal on Quarry Hill, 'so that there is now therein the King's Powder only'. The papers printed it in early September among reports of the crowds that gathered at Cambridge on 2 September. The letter's own words, as printed by others; the excerpts end before it names militia officers.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The resolves of the delegates of the towns of Suffolk County, Massachusetts Bay, 6–9 September 1774 (the Suffolk resolves)
new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolves of a convention of delegates of every town and district of Suffolk County: 'At a meeting of the Delegates of every town and district in the county of Suffolk on Tuesday the 6th of September, at the house of Mr. Richard Woodward of Dedham, and by adjournment at the house of Mr. Vose of Milton, on Friday the ninth instant ... the following being several times read, and put paragraph by paragraph, was unanimously voted'; the resolves declare 'That no obedience is due from this province to either or any part of the acts above mentioned, but that they be rejected as the attempts of a wicked administration to enslave America', recommend that the people appear under arms at least once every week, and recommend withholding all commercial intercourse with Great Britain, Ireland and the West Indies. Several papers print them as they were laid before the Continental Congress at Philadelphia, which approved them on 17 September. The convention's own resolves.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Continental Congress at Philadelphia, September and October 1774: its resolutions, its association and its declaration of 14 October
new_groups.definition: Four papers of the Congress of delegates of the colonies that met at Philadelphia from 5 September 1774, as the papers printed them: its resolution of 22 September asking the merchants to send no more orders to Great Britain, its resolves of 8 October approving the opposition of Massachusetts Bay to the late acts, its declaration and resolves of 14 October, and its Association. Contains those four groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Congress's resolution of 22 September 1774: the merchants not to send any orders for goods to Great Britain
new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolution of the Congress of 22 September 1774: 'Resolved unanimously, That the Congress request the merchants and others, in the several colonies, not to send to Great-Britain any orders for goods, and to direct the execution of all orders already sent to be delayed or suspended, until the sense of the Congress, on the means to be taken for the preservation of the liberties of America, is made public', with the secretary's attestation. The Massachusetts Spy prints it again in December with the Congress's proceedings. The Congress's own resolution.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Congress's resolves of 8 October 1774: it approves the opposition of the inhabitants of Massachusetts Bay to the late acts of Parliament
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Congress's resolution of 8 October 1774: 'Resolved, That the Congress approve of the opposition, by the inhabitants of the Massachusetts-Bay, to the execution of the late Acts of Parliament, and if the same shall be attempted to be carried into execution by force, that in such case all America ought to support them in their opposition', printed with its resolves of 10 and 11 October. The papers print it in two forms: from Philadelphia, under the date of the session, in October, and in the printed extracts of the Congress's proceedings ('Resolved, That this Congress do approve of the opposition made by the inhabitants of the Massachusetts-Bay'), from late October; counted together (C-02), and printed again counts again (C-08). Rind's Virginia Gazette prints the extracts too, but its transcriptions lack the resolution's opening, so that printing is not counted (C-06). The Congress's own resolves.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Congress's declaration and resolves of 14 October 1774: 'Whereas, since the close of the last war, the British Parliament claiming a power of right to bind the people of America, by statute in all cases whatsoever'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the declaration and resolves that the Congress adopted on 14 October 1774, at the head of the printed extracts of its proceedings: 'Whereas, since the close of the last war, the British Parliament claiming a power, of right to bind the people of America, by statute in all cases whatsoever, hath in some acts expressly imposed taxes on them'; it lists the acts of Parliament the colonies complain of, and resolves that the inhabitants of the English colonies in North America 'are entitled to life, liberty, and property: and they have never ceded to any sovereign power whatever, a right to dispose of either without their consent', and to the rights, liberties and immunities of free and natural-born subjects within the realm of England. The Congress's own declaration.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Association of the Continental Congress, October 1774: no importation from Great Britain or Ireland after 1 December 1774
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Association that the delegates signed at Philadelphia: 'We his Majesty's most loyal subjects, the Delegates of the several Colonies of New-Hampshire, Massachusetts-Bay, Rhode-Island, Connecticut, New-York, New-Jersey, Pennsylvania, the three Lower Counties of New-Castle, Kent, and Sussex, on Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North-Carolina, and South-Carolina ... avowing our allegiance to his Majesty, our affection and regard for our fellow subjects in Great-Britain and elsewhere'; its articles bind them, from 1 December 1774, not to import goods from Great Britain or Ireland and the other goods it names, nor to 'import nor purchase any slave imported after the first day of December next', and its eleventh article directs that a committee be chosen in every county, city and town to see it observed. The papers that print its eleventh article again by itself are not counted again (C-07). The delegates' own Association.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Boston, October 1774: the members chosen for the General Court meet at Salem without the governor, and resolve themselves into a provincial congress
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Boston report of October 1774, printed with the members' resolves: 'Wednesday last the members chosen in consequence of Governor Gage's writ for calling a General Assembly, met at the court-house in Salem pursuant to the precepts; and after waiting a day without being admitted to the usual oath, which should have been administered by the Governor or other constitutional officers; and having chosen the Honourable John Hancock, Esq; to be their Chairman ... they proceeded to business, and passed the following Resolves'; the resolves, dated at Salem on 7 October, say that the governor's proclamation discharging them was unconstitutional, and resolve that they form a provincial congress, to meet at Concord. A Boston paper's report, with the members' own resolves.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Vienna, 3 August 1774: 'a courier arrived here with the news of peace between Russia and the Porte'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the European news, from the London Gazette: 'Vienna, August 3. This day at noon a courier arrived here with the news of peace between Russia and the Porte having been concluded on the 17th of July, at the head quarters at Buyuk Canarochi, and signed, on the part of their respective Sovereigns, by Marshal Count Romanzow, and Achmed Effendi, Chiaga to the Grand Vizir.' A report from Vienna in the London Gazette, in the papers' foreign news.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Gage's answer to the Congress, Boston, 20 October 1774: 'Representations should be made with candour, and matters stated exactly as they stand'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter of General Gage to Peyton Randolph, the president of the Continental Congress, dated Boston, 20 October 1774, in answer to the Congress's letter to him of 10 October: 'Representations should be made with Candour, and Matters stated exactly as they stand. People would be led to believe, from your Letter to me of the 10th Instant, that Works were raised against the Town of Boston, private Property invaded, the Soldiers suffered to insult the Inhabitants'; he answers that 'There is not a single Gun pointed against the Town, no Man's Property has been seized or hurt, except the King's', and that no troops have given less cause for complaint. General Gage's own letter.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The King's proclamation of 30 September 1774 for dissolving the present Parliament and calling another (London Gazette, 1 October)
new_groups.definition: Printings of the King's proclamation, from the London Gazette of 1 October 1774: 'A Proclamation, For dissolving the present Parliament, and declaring the calling of another. George R. Whereas we have thought fit, by and with the advice of our privy council, to dissolve the present Parliament, which now stands prorogued to Tuesday the fifteenth day of November next'; it declares that writs for calling a new Parliament will be issued. The King's own proclamation.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Provincial Congress at Cambridge, 1 December 1774: thanks to the other colonies for their donations to Boston and Charlestown
new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolves of the Provincial Congress of Massachusetts Bay of 1 December 1774: 'In Provincial Congress, Cambridge, December 1, 1774. Whereas the rigorous operation of the Boston Port-bill, the metropolis of this province and the neighbouring town of Charlestown have been brought into a most distressful state; many of the inhabitants being deprived of the means of their subsistence ... if they had not been supported by the free and generous contributions of our sister colonies'; it resolves that the Congress's grateful acknowledgments be returned to the several colonies, whose donations it calls convincing proofs of their attachment to the cause of liberty. The Provincial Congress's own resolves.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Scarborough man of war, sent express from Boston to England in September 1774 and back in December
new_groups.definition: Two reports on the man of war Scarborough, which carried dispatches from Boston to England: a letter from Portsmouth in England of 4 October on her arrival there, and a Boston report of December on her return with dispatches for General Gage. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Portsmouth, England, 4 October 1774: 'Since the Scarborough man of war has arrived from Boston, not one of the men have been suffered to come on shore'
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Portsmouth in England, dated 4 October 1774: 'Since the Scarborough man of war has arrived from Boston, not one of the men have been suffered to come on shore, neither are their friends permitted to go on board'; the writer says that the officers keep everything secret, 'from which it is conjectured that things are worse at Boston than government are willing the public should be acquainted with', and that ships are being got ready for sea. A private letter printed at second hand, with the writer's conjecture.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Boston, December 1774: 'the Scarborough man of war, which went express from hence to England the beginning of September last, returned hither again, with dispatches'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Boston paragraph of early December 1774: 'Last Saturday afternoon the Scarborough man of war, which went express from hence to England the beginning of September last, returned hither again, with dispatches for General Gage, the contents of which have not transpired'; it reports that three ships of the line, a frigate and a sloop of war, with 500 marines on board each of the large ships, were said to be about to sail for Boston. The Connecticut Courant prints it in other words ('which was sent express from hence'). A Boston paper's report, partly at second hand ('it was said').
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1774 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1774 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 692 items found on the pages, 259 in 4 or more papers by the finder's count), and again with the families of 1773 over the 1774 pages (items_from_1773.json: 23 items, none in 4 or more). Every item in 3 or more papers was compared by machine with every page and counted again by its opening; a sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers found 2,025 passages in 775 runs, and the runs no finder item covers were read (184 at first; after a fault in the first coverage check was fixed on 24 November, 122 runs are uncovered, all read). Counted item by item, 214 items meet the bar (count_1774.md). Every eligible item within two papers of the papers that survive for its weeks was searched for in the missing papers; the admitted and chosen items were counted with phrase searches over all 1,205 pages in both transcriptions and read on every page.
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN, as amended on 23 November 2026, the owner's choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; as in R-01, the eligible items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, and the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35); one affair's items as in X-1800-01; digests are not admitted; sub-stories (C-01), private persons (R-04) and the list of items read and not admitted (R-03) as in every year. In 1774 5 to 7 papers survive for any item's weeks, so the bar is 4 papers for every item.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1774 has 8 catalogue series, which are 7 papers (C-04): the Connecticut Courant is sn82016376 to 24 May and sn82016139 (The Connecticut Courant and Hartford Weekly Intelligencer) from 7 June. Five papers run all year; Rind's Virginia Gazette survives for 13 January and from 21 April; the Pennsylvania Journal for 27 July only. 5 to 7 papers are in print in any three weeks. No 1774 issue has a corrected date; the release's map lists 5 misfiled RevX pages, on which no admitted printing stands. The Courant to 31 May is dated by weeks and filed under the first date (X-1774-12).
